title: The Friars, fancy-dress balls and talent scouts
summary: Green says he was better in the March of Time days, friendly with dancers at the Friars' parties, and talent scouts hunted tap finds such as Eleanor Powell.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Were you as great a dancer, as you were just back in the '30's? I mean, could you do the same kind of things then, or have you really over the years --
Developed or --

Even more so, I must admit. I think I was much, much better in the days of March of Times, you see. Because I had to be, you see. I was trying to acquire popularity and I became great friends with most of the tap dancers that was here and appearing in New York City. We used to have what they called fancy-dress balls, you see.
(Recording interruption)
What's that?

Well, it became the Performer's Club. It was here at the -- it was developed by the Friar's, you know. The Friar's were very important stars and people of show business -- the entertainment profession. We had to bring into the profession different works of the art of tap dancing, because that was coming the known -- the different author -- they call them playwrights today. They're known as -- and these talent scouts would have such great demands when they come upon a discovery, you know, like a find. They used to use the words sensational new find, you see, and that would become a
personality, you see.
Who were some of those sensational new finds? Some of the performers?
Oh, there were several of them. There was -- especially her -- I mean, she still goes today, that's this Lucille Ball, you know, the dazzling redhead, see. And Rita Hayworth, you see.
But were they looking for tap dancers?
Huh?
Were they looking for tap dancers?
They tap danced.
No, but were the talent scouts that you were talking about looking for tap dancers, primarily?

Yes, yes, yeah, sure. All kinds there was. You see, they'd look -- you know what kind they would look, see, because there was this great variety in tap dancing, see. And the most fashionable ones were the ones that they tried to come upon, because they had to do their jobs too.
And what tap dancers did they find?
Well, like I was saying, they found Eleanor Powell, you know.
Was she a tap dancer?
Yes, yeah, yeah. Yes, she was. The greatest -- the world's greatest of all time.
Initially, though, did she start out as a tap dancer?

No, no. As a champion -- she started out as -- she was developed for championship dancing, you know, and that was a family thing, you see. I think she's an only child, you see. And that's the way it was. I think her father -- he was some kind of producer or something, you know. Very important person at the time. When she was a young one, a little girl, you see. Like Arthur Lake, you see. He was another one, you see -- tap dancer, and he became -- he played Dagwood and Harold T., like that, you know.
